utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, I'm Tom Hannis along with Sebastiaan van Hooydonk.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mico Stanisic, Slobodan Cvijetic and Ms. Deirdre Montgomery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Miroslav Cuskic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And could the witness be escorted back to the stand, unless there is --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: While he is coming in, Your Honour, just regarding scheduling. I said yesterday I thought I would finish at the end of one session. Having assembled my notes last night and finding a couple things I missed, I may request an additional 20 to 30 minutes. I'm still confident that we will finish this witness completely today, and we may finish early. We may finish an hour early, we may finish by noon, but in that regard I've had discussions with Mr. Krgovic about the next witness and I think he's not feeling particularly well, and we would prefer not to start the next witness until Monday if that's agreeable with the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And, Mr. Hannis, we are advised that you would still be within your eight hours even with the extension, but the important thing is that this witness is finished today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: As usual, I remind you of your solemn declaration before I invite Mr. Hannis to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I wanted to start this morning with just a brief question about the time-period between the take-over by the Serbs on the 30th of April and the attack on Prijedor by Muslim forces on the 30th of May. On Tuesday when talking about that, you mentioned that when you were providing some additional information you said: "This is connected with the attack itself. If I talked only about it, then it would seem that it came out of the blue, and that's not true. There were preparations ongoing." And you went on to talk about seeing Dr. Sakovic or Sadikovic, I'm not sure what name is in the transcript here.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sadikovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, travelling up the -- every day the hill so that the Muslims would organise themselves. I want to show you a document that I think relates to that. It's Exhibit P653, tab 41 in the Prosecution binder. Can you read that on the screen all right or do you need a hard copy?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I can read this copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you'll see this is dated the 18th of May, 1992, from Chief Drljaca to Banja Luka, and apparently it's reporting on I would -- what I would call intelligence about the Muslim forces and what weapons they might have. So that seems to kind of support what you were saying that there were preparations ongoing by the Muslims, but it also indicates that Prijedor SJB was monitoring the situation. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before answering, I'd like to say the following. You mentioned the last name of Sadikovic and failed to mention the first name. There were two Sadikovics. Two days ago I mentioned Avdo Salihovic [as interpreted] who worked alongside my wife but this is not the Sadikovic. The one who was an inspector whom I mentioned in the context of the police, that is Avdo Salihovic in the police. The other one was a physician, Eso Sadikovic, and they seem to be holding him in high regard these days. When I said that Sadikovic went across the bridge and up the hill, I didn't mean the policeman but the doctor, just in order to avoid any confusion. Let's go back to what you asked me about initially. Let me have another cursory look. I was listening to your question but let me just go through the dispatch briefly. Can you tell me exactly what is it that you want me to discuss, just your question briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No -- your previous answer that we talked about, you were saying preparations were ongoing, and I'm saying this document suggests to me that the police in Prijedor were aware that the Muslims were preparing something. And this is an example of the fact that they were trying to keep an eye on them and know what was going on. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They both knew, both sides. Let me give you an example. I just thought about it the other day. It resembled when the United States and the Soviet Union were trying to reach the moon first. They both knew they were on the right track, but they couldn't exactly pin-point how far ahead each of them was. We all knew -- well, conditionally I say "we all knew," I mean the people knew that there were preparations underway, but there was no direct communication between the sides. One could observe the preparations, but I don't think anyone had complete information about the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I accept that. I think you mentioned also in the communications centre before the attack on the 30th of May, you were hearing some -- over the radio some information about negotiations that were going on between the Serbs and the Muslims. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that. What I did say is that on the 9th of April, the chief arrived and he summoned the two of us. I don't think I ever said that I listened to the radio. I know that he gave them the task of broadcasting that and I could hear it, but that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: There is a problem with the interpretation, so can Mr. Hannis pose the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It was my understanding that you had said earlier between -- between the 29th of April and -- or the 30th of April and the 30th of May that in the communications centre on occasion you overheard some talk on police radio about negotiations that were going on between the Serbs and the Muslims; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I wasn't clear about your initial question. When you said "radio," I thought you had in mind the radio station in Prijedor, but this is the ultra high frequency radio waves of the police. I wasn't listening in all the time --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I don't know what exactly you want me to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But speaking of Radio Prijedor, I think you told us you don't have a radio at home and you didn't listen to the radio in 1992, 1993, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at home. But I never turn it on. I have one in my car, but I usually listen to music.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I take it then you never heard a radio broadcast in 1994 where Simo Miskovic, the former SDS president, president of the municipality, talked about the events regarding the take-over on 30th --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simo Miskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah. You didn't hear him on Radio Prijedor talking about the take-over and that happened on May 30th?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now I want to ask you about Keraterm and Omarska. At page 24815 you mentioned that after the attack on the 30th of May a number of Muslims had been taken prisoner, and pretty soon the numbers were so big that there wasn't room to keep them in the detention facilities available in Prijedor at the SJB. And Keraterm and later Omarska were used for that purpose. I have a question based on something you said when you testified about this in the Stakic case. Do you remember testifying in 2003 in the Tribunal here in Mr. Stakic's trial?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember being at the Tribunal, but I no longer remember what I said then. Perhaps you can jog my memory. In any case, I always try to say what I think and what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. At page 10695 on the 20th of January, 2003, you were asked by I think the Defence lawyer, Mr. Lukic: "Was an investigation centre set up because of the increased numbers of detainees, that is, Omarska and Keraterm?" And your answer was: "Yes, I know that they were set up. I didn't participate in that. I don't know who set them up and how, but yes, at that time, they were set up. Personally I didn't believe that that was the reason for setting that up -- for setting them up, but I can't tell you." My question was: Why did you not believe that was the reason for setting them up? What did you think the reason was?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I believe you when you say that this is what's in the transcript. First of all, I no longer remember what I said, but I do believe it is true and I maintain that opinion. I can repeat everything I said then and then we can go back to what you mentioned. First of all, I don't know what I said then. I never read the transcript. I do know that the opinion I had then has not changed. Nothing influenced any change of that opinion. I know that neither at the time nor nowadays anyone tried to influence my opinion, any of the parties here. I have no reason to tell you something that is not true. Given all that and given the fact that my opinion has not changed, I can tell you that -- I'll try to be more precise so do bear with me. Maybe I'll go off on a tangent and you can bring me back. First of all, why were there no arrests before the attack on Prijedor? There were only a few arrests, but there were no collection centres in existence yet. Whatever premises existed before were used at that time until the 30th of April -- sorry, May, when the attack on Prijedor occurred. What happened then? There was the attack and the army arrived driving those Muslims out, those who had attacked. I saw women and children going the other way led by some Kiki, the barber, he was asking for assistance. So there were no gathering or collecting of population en masse. I could hear fighting in the distance, but close to the market, which doesn't really tell you much, anyone who knows Prijedor knows what I'm talking about, I could see a hundred women and children coming there, not small children but teenagers I would say. So they were moving. Following that I could observe -- I wasn't informed because there were no collegium meetings. Decisions were being made at lower levels and this is what I could observe in the field. The extent of my inclusion was, for example, Simo arriving telling me, "Go and set up a phone line in Keraterm," and I did. The network was down and I didn't do that directly because it was part of the work of the telecommunications company. However, I needed their permission, et cetera, et cetera. So I was there to provide a service, and I could see a lot of people gathering there. I didn't analyse the situation, but I couldn't go through without noticing. That is why I know -- let me digress a bit. When you mentioned Nusret Sivac, we moved on to another topic but there is one thing which is very important. He is a typical example of some things which took place concerning this context. Nusret Sivac was taken not on the first day but a few days later. And then he stayed for one night only and came back or maybe two days and then came back. Then he spent a period at home and then was taken again and then returned, say, a month later. It was then that I helped him to go to Germany or wherever it was that he went to. What does it mean? It means that they were being processed. It means that he wasn't taken away the first time around, but he was taken away when information arrived that he should be interrogated. After that he was released because I guess their conclusion was that he was not guilty. Later on they concluded that he should be brought in yet again. Let me try to slow down for the sake of the interpreters. And then Sivac left again, which means that there must have been gauging going on as part of the application of the Law on Criminal Procedure. There may have been mistakes, transgressions, people even being killed. There was unrest, but another thing. Why is Nusret Sivac a typical example --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- just one moment. Please bear with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nusret Sivac was a civilian officially, and whoever wants to use his example will say that they didn't only bring in soldiers but citizens as well. But once I asked Sivac: "Why were you in the cafe Obala when the attack occurred?" This was the epicentre of fighting. And he said, "Boss, I had my own poker machine in the bar. I came to collect." It may be true, it may not be true, but he was in the wrong place at the wrong time. So he wasn't just another ordinary civilian at the time. Now perhaps we can go back to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, let me ask another question because what I was trying to understand was what you thought was the reason for these camps being set up. But let me ask you this: This is something -- I'm going to read you something that Mr. Zupljanin is reported to have said on July 11th, 1992, at a meeting of the RS MUP senior officials. This is from Exhibit P160, tab 77, and he said: "The army and Crisis Staffs or War Presidencies are requesting that as many Muslims as possible are gathered, and they are leaving these undefined camps up to the internal affairs organs. Conditions in these camps are bad, there's no food, some individuals do not observe international norms because, among other things, such collection centres are not adequate or there are other reasons." Now, that sounds like a fair description of what was happening in Prijedor with the setting up of Keraterm and Omarska. Would you agree or not or do you not have enough information to say one way or another?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last thing you said, the last few sentences when you quoted Mr. Zupljanin. I'm not 100 per cent familiar with it, but it does partially tally with my opinion. As for the last thing you asked me about, let me try to explain. I know I'm trying to tell the truth. Perhaps, though, there may have been a detail that I related to in the sense of expanding and I may have said that. I'll try to go back and recall what I said or perhaps you can remind me. I hope I'm not going insane yet, but I don't know exactly what happened. I am convinced, though, that that was true as is what I'm saying now. I speak a lot and I don't wrap things up nicely. And even now I get corrections in rhetorical sense. I will try again to recall if you can read out the last sentence again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The last sentence of what Mr. Zupljanin said?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Zupljanin, what I said in the previous trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Again, reading from Stakic at 10 --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just the last thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: 10695. "Personally, I didn't believe that that was the reason for setting them up, but I can't tell you." And the question that was put to you was --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All is clear. All is clear. I understand the question now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute. I'll try. From this point in time I can see that the collection centre, as they referred to it, was simply used because it was a larger area where they could exercise their legal authority. I told you there was a small detention room and then there was a larger area. And it strikes me as the situation being exactly that. I guess I said what I said. No one made it up. I have no doubts about that. But I'm trying to say what it was that I was trying to say at the time. I don't see it. I don't see the logic. There -- it's a larger area and the processing continued. It's another matter in what ways and whether those involved were of sufficient professional background to do it properly. In any case, at a first glance it seemed that everything was in keeping with the law, but they did have more work on their hands. I no longer know exactly what I meant when I said that. Perhaps if I had time to ponder I'd be able to recall and if I do, I'll certainly tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let me ask you a couple more things about the camps from your Stakic testimony. At page 10698 you were talking about the investigations in Omarska and Keraterm and you said, talking about Omarska: "I saw in Omarska our inspectors. And when I say 'our,' I mean the employees of the public security station in Prijedor." And then about eight lines on you say: "In Keraterm, now likewise, but fewer of them all together, a fewer number of people." So if I understand correctly, police inspectors from Prijedor SJB were working in Omarska and Keraterm in 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do believe I said what you just quoted because I still think that way. When I was in Keraterm, I was by a telephone set and there was somebody coming - was it the Red Cross or UNHCR? - at any rate, the whole thing was a bit window-dressed, if you know what I mean. Everybody appeared in a much nicer light than was the case. I can't say that everybody enjoyed their stay there because that would not have been the truth, but it wasn't as bad as that. They spent some 20 minutes there. I don't know if that day that I spent in Keraterm there was Omarska already as a camp because Keraterm predated Omarska. I do know that there were larger accommodation premises in Keraterm. And when I mentioned inspectors I meant, of course, those from the Prijedor station, but there were a great deal of those others who were either members of the army or came from elsewhere and were not members of the SJB Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The other inspectors who were not from the army but came from elsewhere, do you know where they came from? Were any of them from Banja Luka CSB, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did say that in my last answer, that they were people I didn't know. So I would be mistaken now to tell you anything further.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One other question from your Stakic testimony, the Prosecutor, Mr. Koumjian asked you at page 10739, he said: "Sir, it was common knowledge in Prijedor that in July there was a massacre at the Keraterm camp; isn't that correct?" And your answer, Mr. Jankovic, was: "I heard that it had happened. That's what I heard. I didn't witness anything nor did I go there at this time. Who I heard it from, I don't remember. But the way people talked about those things -- you know, at work, no one talked about this. Everyone just sort of kept silent. But there was a general sense of horror. And then whenever someone brought the subject up they would just say, 'Yeah, it happened,' and then people would just be very worried, concerned. No one was enthusiastic about this." That's what you said then. Is that still the way you remember it now?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall it at all, but when I do read it now, I see that I explained it much better than I would be able to explain it now to you. Sorry, if you can just look at what I'm motioning now. This is the way everybody said, motioning to their mouth, as in stay mum. Don't speak about it. So that is how everybody motioned, this way. That was the sort of information that was passed around. Somebody was there, but I didn't -- it didn't even cross my mind to go and ask who was on the list because I might end up on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For the record the motion you were indicating to me is you were holding up your hand in front of your mouth vertically like this or now you're holding up one finger, and keep quiet, don't say anything?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one finger in front of your mouth, and that's a sign for keep quiet, shut up, and that's what a colleague would say to a colleague. I'm not saying it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand. All right. Continuing on on page 24817 of our transcript, on Tuesday you mentioned when you went out to Omarska to install a radio and when you got ready to go back it was already dark. You said: "The police told me that I couldn't leave at that time because the buses with the detainees were just arriving." So you parked and waited until that operation was completed and then you travelled about midnight back home. Do you remember approximately when that was? Do you know the month?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the first day of Omarska. Now what date was that? Well, after the 30th of May. It must have been early June.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't keep track of dates. At any rate, the date when Omarska came into being such as it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember how many buses of detainees were brought and unloaded that night? Any idea?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never got out of my car, the Golf I had. And of course I'm saying "I" all the time, but there was a technician who had been there with me and he followed in my every footstep and he was a driver normally, but this once I was behind the wheel. And since I expected that there would be a lot of traffic there, I switched into reverse and parked by a bus. I had this Golf, blue one, of the police anyway. So I parked behind the bus and darkness was setting in already. And as I parked behind the bus, I was out of any artificial illumination because the building itself had its lighting. And -- just a moment, let me give you this one detail. Let's say this is the gate. Two buses were parked in like this, and those that were arriving were passing this way by them, and I was unable to see who was coming in because I was at the other side of the bus. I never saw those who were coming in. I didn't see where they were coming from, and to tell you the truth I didn't really feel the need to count how many buses there were. I saw at one point a person in a blue T-shirt bolting away from there. He was fleeing. And then I heard gun-fire, and that of course caused me to duck, in fact, and stay motionless. And as I said, I stayed there -- well, I told you about it. It wasn't midnight, it was before midnight. I probably came home at midnight. And let me be precise. I may have been a bit vague about it the last time. The prisoners were not done getting off the buses yet and the -- there was this -- next to mine there was this blue police Golf. At one point I could see that the lights were on and a charge -- or the commander was in the car. He started the car and went out of the compound. I couldn't see but I could sense that he was going out of the main gate and I wanted -- at one point I thought perhaps I should follow him because he had his rotating light on, and I did that. As I quickly started my car, he was perhaps already 50 metres away from me because he was driving pretty quickly. And since I wasn't really familiar with the area, I came across a junction, an intersection. There were no houses there, and I turned left and realised that this was a blind alley because at some point the road simply disappeared. And you don't go to Prijedor through Omarska, or rather, through Kozarac. And as I missed the right turn, because I told you there were two turns there, I came across some farmers there, peasants, and that's where we were mistreated. That's the bit that I related. So I may have seen half or a third or perhaps two-thirds of the prisoners as they were coming out. It's difficult for me to assess the amount of time I spent there. And since it was an uncomfortable situation, it seemed to me like an eternity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in your answer on Tuesday you said: "The police told me:" You "couldn't leave." So was it the police who were dealing with the arrival of the buses and taking the prisoners off, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were all sorts there. Some of them were members of the local Omarska substation, so I knew them. There was also Cigo with some of his men. I'm sure that I saw him for the first time then, and I don't think I ever saw him after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The name you just mentioned, who was he and who he was working for?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was one of their lot, a villager of Omarska. I suppose he worked in the mine, though he did wear a camouflage uniform at the time. I suppose he was deployed to the front line in Slavonia and it was a pretty frayed uniform and there were two more men with him. They were more of his -- they were more his escorts rather than anything else. Cigo was swearing at our policemen. "Why have you come here? Who is it you have brought here? Give us a list. You don't have a list." He wants to kill them. And he asked me, "Who are you?" I was in civilian clothes. He [as interpreted] said, "I am a communications officer." He says, "What the hell are you doing here?" So I just kind of slunk into my car. He was shooing everyone away. I was -- I felt a bit privileged for being a communications officer. But there you are. How is it that you can feel in such circumstances? There were far fewer policemen compared to all manner of individuals who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you a couple more questions on camps. I want to show you some documents. The first one is tab 88, it's Exhibit P668. I think you can see this one on the screen. It's a short document. Mr. Jankovic, this is -- I'm sorry, could we go to the next page in the B/C/S. It's dated the 1st of August from Simo Drljaca to Banja Luka CSB. I think you might have been shown it before. It has a --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but from a different perspective. We looked at the format, at the heading, and signature. And I didn't know it then. I don't know it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The information is from Mr. Drljaca that at a meeting on 24 July the War Presidency of Prijedor adopted a decision where the reserve police force that was presently employed should be greatly reduced and security for Keraterm, Trnopolje, and Omarska be provided by the army with a dead-line of the 31st of July. He goes on to say the army refused to assume security duties which our station supplies with a staff of 300 police officers every day. Did you realise that there were that many police officers working at Keraterm, Trnopolje, and Omarska providing security? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I don't know what the actual numbers were. But as I'm looking at it, I have this feeling that individuals such as Simo -- well, yesterday I heard about 5.000 a day -- 300? Well, a station had roughly 120 men at all times, and then Prijedor 2 was a smaller station, under 100 -- well, this means that all of the police force should have been there, which isn't true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Do you know how many reserve policemen were activated by or after the 30th of April in Prijedor municipality? Do you have any idea about what those numbers were?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not just I that don't have an idea, nobody does. Why? Let's say a commander would take on his neighbour to make sure that he isn't deployed to the front line somewhere, so it changed frequently --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and I really don't know how it was that they were officially admitted. There were an official list, an earlier list, that had been agreed to by the Muslims, as I said. Later on that list was --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. But you would agree with me, wouldn't you, that the chief, Mr. Drljaca, was in a better position than you were as the comms chief to know how many reserve policemen Prijedor had because that was his job; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a boss. He was reported to. Nobody reported to me. I was only asked to provide a radio set and a battery. Regardless, this yesterday's figure of 5.000, and this today's figure, I don't think that they are realistic at all from how I viewed the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, we'll look at some documents later and I'll ask you some further questions. But for now, if you would just note the number of this dispatch at the top, 2169, remember that number because I want to show you the next one --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which number? How would I remember it? Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I want you to remember it right now for the next minute before I show you the next document. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. 2169. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Because there's a note on here about --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My memory's full already, but all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to show you tab 93. This is Exhibit P1682. And I will tell you, this is dated the 4th of August, 1992, from Chief Zupljanin to Prijedor SJB to the chief. And you see it says regarding your dispatch 11-12-2169/92. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- which number is it you're reading? There's quite a few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, that's the one --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A moment -- 11-12-2169/92. Fine. That's the one from before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Right. And the chief, Chief Zupljanin, says: "Regarding your dispatch, number above, we agree that, for the reasons cited in said dispatch, you may postpone the obligation of co-ordinating the number of reserve policemen ... until further notice, that is, until adequate solutions are found together with the appropriate commands of the army of the Serbian Republic in accordance with the decisions of the War Presidency of Prijedor ..." So it seems like chief Zupljanin is agreeing in Prijedor Mr. Drljaca doesn't have to reduce the number of reserve policemen yet because they're still needed to do the security duty at Keraterm, Omarska, and Trnopolje until something can be worked out with the army. That's what it means, isn't it? Is that how you read it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, let's not talk about how things seem to me. You probably know them now better than I did at the time. What they were doing, what sort of information they were handling, what sort of respect they had for each other, I don't think they had respect -- much respect for anyone, including Mr. Zupljanin. What was in their mind -- well, I wasn't able to and I'm not able to assume anything. And to ask me about how things seemed to me now, let me not talk about it. What it seemed to me is that this was just Simo's rattle. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But he did inform his chief and request permission to not reduce the police force and Zupljanin wrote back and said "okay."

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, my question is: Your 65 ter summary that we got from the Defence indicated that you were going to provide evidence that Mr. Drljaca was, in effect, acting independently, a lone wolf, not taking instructions, not reporting to his boss. And I'm trying to show this as an example where he is informing his boss of the situation and asking permission to do something and getting permission. I guess let me ask you this question: Is it your permission that Mr. Drljaca did not follow directions from Mr. Zupljanin or that he did not report when he was asked to? And if that is your position, can you point us to a specific document or example that shows that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am -- I have the habit of speaking figuratively always. I see that as my children asking for money but then not asking me what they will spend their money on. So are they listening to what I have to say or not? Well, the same was with Simo. Whenever he needed to relieve himself of the burden of responsibility, then he will consult and ask around. Otherwise, if he needed something done, well then -- that's the gist of it in my view, if you agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying. But from --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And we can say that what we've been discussing here just now is in that same context.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But from how you've described your relationship with Mr. Drljaca, it sounds to me as though you weren't in a position to know exactly when and how often and the contents of whatever all his communications with Mr. Zupljanin were because he could have been talking to Mr. Zupljanin on the phone, he could have sent him communications by courier or directly by some other form of hard copies that you didn't see in the communications centre. So you weren't really in a position to know exactly what happened between Mr. Drljaca and Mr. Zupljanin. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Here is an example. The dispatch 2169, I had it in my hand and there's my signature. Now, the dispatch we have on our screens now was typewritten. So what was it? It was a fax. My communication links weren't operating and Simo had a Telefax machine as did the Chief Zupljanin -- I mean, I didn't see it, but if I had one, then he must have had one for sure. So evidently the dispatch that we have on our screens now was transmitted by fax. So I had the question in my hand without ever seeing what the answer was. So the information I had was inaccurate, incomplete, et cetera, when we're talking about this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Different topic. At page 24823 you told us about the occasion where some -- someone who was I think probably under the influence of alcohol, you said, asked you for your ID, thought you were a Muslim. He fired a shot at you, actually. You remember that, I'm sure?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My question is: You didn't report that crime to the police. You didn't file any kind of complaint or make an official report about it, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Why not? I mean -- aren't --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The interpreters asked if you could repeat your answer. I think it was too fast or they didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Such cases were so frequent at the time, not just involving me, that if I mentioned it nobody would have paid it any attention. It's as if I were here reporting about it raining in The Hague -- well, it rains all the time. And the individual was Dragan Fustar. I didn't know his name at the time. I learned it later. He passed away in the meantime and it was because of alcohol. He wasn't that old. I saw him for the first time then and I only learned his name later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Dragan Fustar, is that the name you said?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's spelled correctly here. It's not an S but a Sh, but fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Do you know who he was affiliated with in terms -- was he a policeman? Was he in the army? Was he in the intervention platoon? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He had a camouflage military uniform. I have no idea what unit he belonged to. He was definitely not with the police, definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You also mention another man I think the other day, Zoran Zigic, am I pronouncing his name correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are. If you said Z, Z with a diacritic, then it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's what I meant to say. I don't know if I did it correctly. Did you ever see him --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you see him around or in the Prijedor SJB in 1992 on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used to see him a lot in the vicinity of the SJB as well, but never on a regular basis. That guy must have been everywhere. He did go to the SJB at the beginning in the course of the first few days, but who it was that he worked with and what he was doing, that's something I don't know. I do know, though, that the policemen beat him once. They beat him up well, but he didn't seem to mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Just a couple of questions about salary. You mentioned at page 24827 that the municipality was where the police were being paid or by whom the police were being paid. I want to ask you, I know you're an electrical engineer and not an accountant, but what do you know about the SDK, the public accounting service in Prijedor? Do you know how moneys were channelled to or through the SDK from higher levels of the government like the republic level or the regional level? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't. From all -- out of all aspects of life, that's the one I understand the least, not even today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to touch on a few communications documents before I go to the last two reports. Tab number 55 is Exhibit P468. This is just a technical question about means of communication. I think you can just look at the screen because I only have a question about the headings and addresses. This is a document that appears to be sending conclusions of the ARK Crisis Staff, and it appears to be going through Sanski Most. Do you see that stamp in the upper right-hand corner? Can we enlarge that.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now my English translation says that ECV, those first three letters stand for the Electronic Communications Centre. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what the abbreviation stands for. As for any electronic communications centre, I don't know whether it existed. Even nowadays they're not on good terms with the electronics, let alone back then. I don't know what it means. I do know that OSNO means the Municipal Secretariat for All People's Defence in Sanski Most. It was sent by Telefax. This had nothing to do with me. It never did, not documents like this one or similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could we zoom out so we can see the entire width of the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You see there's a fax header with a telephone number and then the abbreviation COB, Bosanski Novi. Do you know what the abbreviation COB stands for there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you see the line with --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it all well, but I can't find COB.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You see the -- there's the date and time and a telephone number and then straight across COB BOS NOVI?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it. The entire line, including the COB, is the data that the piece of equipment prints out. It's either in the -- in its own memory or in the memory of the switchboard. The COB is something that the fax machine is affiliated with, a particular office. We can see the sending time, page 1, the date. It was all done by the machine. Here is the number. I don't know, though, what COB means. Obviously the Telefax machine was part of that institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. So that's what I call the fax header on the top of the page?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. If that's what you call it, then that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I only show this to you because we had some discussion before about whether you were aware of the existence of other communications systems in the municipalities and it seems the Ministry of Defence or the National Defence, whatever it was called, in Republika Srpska at the time had a system separate and apart from the police communications system; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about other systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's take Prijedor. I don't know anything about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. That's --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had nothing to do with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's fine. Let me show you tab 56 which is Exhibit P656. I can hand you a hard copy of this one. It's a little longer. It's dated the 29th of May, 1992, the day before the attack. And it's from Chief Drljaca to Banja Luka CSB, responding to some communication from them the day before, the 28th. And it's providing information about the various activities of the police and the number of policemen and the number of police stations, et cetera. I want to ask you about the last paragraph. It says: "The previous war structure anticipated 630 policemen. The new war structure, which is functioning now, was prepared during secret preparations for the take-over." And we talked about this before. I think you said when you got to Cirkin Polje on the night of the 29th and you saw all the people there and you got the stack of ID cards that had already been printed out, you thought to yourself: How long has this been going on? Why wasn't I aware of this? This is consistent with that - right? - that there were secret preparations that had been going on for some time before the take-over. That just confirms what you thought, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What was your question exactly? I answered yes to the very last part of what you said. Is there anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, that's all. I just wanted to ask if that was consistent with the conclusion you had reached. Let me show you one more, this is tab --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to have any miscommunication. The number of 1.342 members, in my view it's nonsense, it's impossible. Next he says that there were 180 active-duty police officers. And before the war the number never went beyond 150. If some of them were Muslim, how could they have had so many active-duty policemen? Some did arrive from Croatia after leaving the police force there, but this figure is unrealistic. Perhaps you can documents to corroborate this that I'm not familiar with. I wasn't interested in that and I wasn't at any meetings where this was discussed. But in my view, this is ... From my point of view as a communications person, I can tell you that each pair of policemen had one hand-held radio, which means that there should have been 650 hand-held radios to cover all these men -- well, no, there weren't as many in the time of war. Maybe there were 60 or 70 of them. Certainly not a hundred men with hand-held radios. That's speaking from my point of view. This seems a gigantic figure, but I don't know what the real situation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. Let me show you one more or two more before the break. Tab 85. I think this is 65 ter number 491. I think you can read this one on the screen. It's fairly short. Now, this is Chief Drljaca I guess noting that they had received a particular dispatch from Chief Zupljanin from Banja Luka CSB, in which Zupljanin ordered all SJB chiefs to do their best to establish and maintain communications systems. It says: "Resolve all problems relating to this order with the Banja Luka CSB comms department and KZ, cryptographic protection, and the local ... post office." It goes on to say: "I especially insist that a KT, short wave, communication be established and maintained daily with IC-751 radio stations which all municipalities have ..." Did you know about this and was that done in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall this. I guess this dispatch did arrive. I can only presume what it's all about, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say this. This type of device, IC-751, it's a Japanese short wave piece of equipment. And yesterday I explained what a KT or short wave equipment is. It's something that we fell back on when all else failed. I suppose Rakovic proposed this because he wasn't well acquainted with communications, although he was a chief of communications. I'm surprised that Simo Drljaca took his word for it. Using this would be like having policemen train in riding bikes with the war looming from my point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. My question is, though: Did you have those daily communications?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I think part of the witness's answer is missing because he mentioned that -- something about implementation of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you hear that, Witness, and could you answer for us if that was implemented in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My fault. I got tangled up a bit. No importance was attached to it because it made no sense. It couldn't cover functional realities. There were very few people working in communications and they couldn't even handle the tasks they already had. Let me illustrate. It would be as if you were making construction workers do pushups. It was nonsensical.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Illogical.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Let me show you one more before our break. It's tab 92, the Exhibit number is P669. And I'll hand you a hard copy of this one. When you have this in your hand you'll see it's dated the 4th of August, 1992, from Chief Drljaca to Banja Luka CSB. Certain information being provided pursuant to a request that originally came from the Ministry of the Interior examine and then from a dispatch from CSB. I want to ask you about item number (b), it's on page 2 of the B/C/S, so it's the next page over. And Mr. Drljaca is reporting that: "Members of the active and the reserve police force, practically alone and without a fight, took over in Prijedor, sealed off the town, and organised the security of all vital structures." And the next paragraph says: "After the outbreak of fighting, they took an active part and showed an impressive level of cohesion and synchronisation with members of the military. In May, almost all of the policemen from Prijedor, Omarska, Lamovita, and Tukovi participated in the fighting, first in Hambarine then in Kozarac and Prijedor ..." Now, I think you told me before that you believe that police were not involved in fighting in those areas in May because you didn't see any evidence of it from your position in the communications department. Nobody was asking you for communications support. But here the chief says almost all the police from Prijedor were engaged in the fighting. Certainly he would be in a better position to know about that than you were; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Irrespective of the fact that I talk a lot, I seem to omit things. First of all, when I discussed the take-over, I told you there were all sorts of uniforms. I may be colour-blind, but I couldn't go wrong about the crates. None of it belonged to the police. I told you about the major and the other guy who asked for a hand-held radio, they were not police. I can give you many examples in a brush-stroke way. If I sat down I would come up with many more. On the other hand --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there because I don't disagree with you about that. I think Mr. Drljaca is pumping up the role of the police in the take-over and failing to admit the involvement --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, ignoring the involvement of the army --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who, he the boss? Yeah, he'd say: "I freed Prijedor alone."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the police was far smaller in numbers. But when all this was ongoing it wasn't that the military was doing all the work and the policemen were sitting back having a cigarette. They had their own tasks but I didn't know which. I wasn't privy to that, I wasn't interested. I do know, however, that they didn't sit in their living-rooms and they were not looking for chicken thieves. However, I really can't say what it was that they were doing. It would be irresponsible of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. One last question before the break. If you could go to page 3, the last paragraph, paragraph (g), Mr. Drljaca is saying the following: "A more organised participation of the police in executing possible combat activities is recommended so that police units and formations would in future be subject to the command of the military unit in charge of the combat activities." You see that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You personally don't have any knowledge about the nature of the co-ordination between the police and the army during those operations in Hambarine, Kozarac, and Prijedor earlier in the summer of 1992, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did tell you that the military took part. The very fact that there were two tanks there on the 30th of May confirms that. Yes, they were there generally although I don't know how many. Please do bear in mind that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat this part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Stop. The interpreter just asked if you could repeat that part of your answer, I guess after the fact -- after you said --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will. I apologise. When trying to analyse what he said or thought, one needs to bear in mind that Simo came from the kindergarten. He was a lawyer who worked in kindergartens and schools and then came to the police. No one knows what that man thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Time for our first break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Last sentence which witness said is not recorded. He said it's not real, or something like that. So can you ask the witness to repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, the last sentence we have from your last answer is: "No one knows what that man thought." Mr. Krgovic says there was something additional you said. Can you tell us if there was and what it was?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I said perhaps he is the only one who could know what he thought. All this seems to me to be unrealistic in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before the usher goes too far I'll hand her a copy of the first document I want to show the witness, which is 65 ter number 3517, it's at Prosecution tab 140.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, while this is on the way to you I'll tell you it's dated the 18th of January, 1993. And it's a -- it's the annual report on the status and organisation of crypto graphic data protection at the Prijedor public security station for 1992. And it has your name at the end on the last page. Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that the report that you prepared in 1993 to cover the work that had been done in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I hope I'm not mistaken, but your tab 140 is --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- a different number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I misspoke, Your Honours, it's tab 138.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, there it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, I don't know if you were able to answer while the Judge and I were talking. Do you recognise that? Is that a report you prepared covering the work in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's my report. I wrote it and signed it and I know it. You can ask me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that these kind of reports were fairly typical in the MUP, both I think before the war and after April 1992 when the RS MUP was formed. Often I see them -- there were quarterly reports every three months but there was always an annual report as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only I need to give you an additional explanation so you know everything about it from the start. The document relating the state of affairs and the way encryption was organised, nothing else. It's about people charged with it, equipment, and documents, and I mean these codes, for a given year. The format of the report was prescribed in a military booklet. So you would know that under 1 you need to relate the state of affairs with regard to encryption personnel. And everybody used the same format in the pre-war period because they had gone through training, as had I. And it was something that we took over from the JNA. However, during the war people were admitted who had not been familiar with these issues and may not have applied the format that I always adhered to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The item number 1 is the status of personnel and that lists the people working there and their jobs. Were all the people listed here Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are all of them Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rankovic, that's I, the technician, yes. Devan [phoen] Djukic maintenance technician, yes. Sarac Batinica, Kovrlija Radanac [phoen], Pasic Mackovic [phoen], yes. That's as at the 18th of January, 1993; in other words, it's a report for 1992 -- just a moment. It was written on the 18th of January. It says 18 January and it says here charged with encryption duties with -- in 1992. So it is a report for 1992. Now, the personnel as listed here were present in the beginning of 1992, where Kapuric [phoen] and the Ukrainian who I said fled just before the war were present, but there were some on this list here who were not there at the time. So you could say that sometime in the middle of the year there was a mixed composition of personnel, but the personnel listed here were present at the time of the writing of the report. And one of the men here was from a mixed marriage, but of course this isn't something that would be stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. And then you list the various cryptographic data protection devices and documents and the instructions that you have. If you could go to the last --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That were used under the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. If you could go to the last page, item number 5 is -- in my English translation says: "Communications via telegram in 1991." But then the next line says: "Communication via open and encoded telegrams in 1992 ..." So I'm thinking that's a typo, a typographic mistake, the line that is underlined after number 5.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so as well. It must be a mistake, my mistake because I wrote it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And this is -- so I take it this is the total number of open and encoded telegrams received and sent by Prijedor SJB for the entire year of 1992 going back to 19 -- going back to January 1st?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, because it says "telegrams," and I understand that to mean it's telegrams only. There may have been other kinds of communications from Prijedor SJB and to Prijedor SJB that weren't telegrams. For example, someone may have sent a 20-page manual, instructions about something, by courier. So that's not a telegram but that is a communication. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it's got nothing to do with the communications centre. It wouldn't go through us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. There were some --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the items listed here were the ones handled by us. We had a fax machine as well, but they had one as well so they could use it directly. We did not list the uses of the Telefax here, but besides they would be used by the chief and commander independently of us. And it says here that the total traffic in telegrams in 1992 was reduced by 62 per cent compared to the previous year, to the year before, which wasn't a very busy one either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this document. It's not an exhibit. Back in February 2010 when we had a communications witness from Banja Luka testify, the Prosecution had sought to add this exhibit to our list at that time. But because we hadn't made a motion, Your Honours on the 25th of February, 2010, gave an oral ruling and did not permit the Prosecution to add some 23 end-of-the-year communication reports from various SJBs. But given that this witness is here now and he was called by the Defence to testify about communications in Prijedor, it's his report, I think it's not prejudicial to the Defence and it's not unfair to allow the Prosecutor to tender it as an exhibit at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no objection to the document being admitted. Regardless of the objections I may have stated before, what the Prosecutor said does warrant the admission of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2394. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jankovic, the last document I think that I'm going to show you -- and it's not a log-book, you'll be happy to hear. It's tab number 137, the Exhibit number is P689, and it's a long one so I need to hand you a hard copy of it. Thank you. You'll see by the cover this is a report on the work of the Prijedor SJB during the last nine months of 1992. And it's dated January 1993. If you go to the very last page you'll see it's from Chief Simo Drljaca, maybe on the back side. Have you ever seen this report before?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somebody showed it to me. Was it the Defence or you? Perhaps both. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you have seen it in 1993? I mean, was it common practice for the chief to circulate a copy of the final report to the various department heads so you could see what it looked like or do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Nobody informed us of their own report. We would be copying our report to others, not the other way around ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If we could have up in e-court so we can follow along P689, and if we could go to page 2 in e-court in both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Jankovic, if you could turn the cover page and look at the first page of text there, yes, on your left-hand side, I want to start with a couple of things from those paragraphs. This is the creation of conditions for the functioning of the public security station. And I think it's the third sentence says: "In view of the fact that the Chief of the police security station in Prijedor and the Commander of the Police Station for the control and the safety of traffic were both SDA people, these activities had to be covert and involve a ... limited number of personnel." And he's talking about trying to establish the functioning of a police station under the Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs. So the chief and the commander he's referring to there, that would have been Hasan Talundzic and Fikret Kadiric; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And he says this covert work -- he said: "The work was carried out outside the Station premises, often using the premises of the cultural centre in Cirkin Polje. The focus of the work was on the covert organisation and the formation of 'shadow' police stations and the arming and equipping of personnel. In this manner, 13 police stations were established with a total staff of about 1.500." Now, I take it from everything you've told us so far, you didn't know anything about this; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when you put it all together it all fits with what I said about, for instance, those crates that I saw, then it goes to show that this is probably true, that this was the way things were done. But since I was clueless when I saw those crates, it means that I was clueless about this as well. It does seem realistic to me, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the next paragraph he mentions that activities were launched to prepare for a take-over by force. "These activities gained momentum in April and the actual date of the take-over was forced upon us by the Presidency of the then Socialist Republic of BH, when they issued the order to attack military installations and convoys." That's clearly a reference to that 29 April dispatch that you told us about taking to the meeting and --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. "As a result, in the night between 29 and 30 April, following very detailed preparations and pursuant to the relevant decision of the Executive Committee of the Serbian Municipality of Prijedor, an organised take-over of power was embarked upon. About 400 policemen assembled in the cultural centre ... and at 0400 hours, took control of important sites in the town ..." That part, is that consistent with what you saw on the night of the 29th and the morning of the 30th of April? I think you gave us a lower number of policemen that you saw. I think you said 150 to 200. But otherwise, is it consistent with what you saw?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This isn't impossible. First of all, I came in as the night was falling and I suppose there were others coming after me. I wasn't going out, but what was happening outside of the building? There were -- there was the army and the youths and let me call them those people. When did they come? They didn't go into the building. I didn't go out. And I said that my assessment of the numbers was between 100 and 200. Of course there could have been more. There was room enough, that's for sure. But I didn't go out until the morning hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. If we could go to the next page in e-court in both B/C/S and English. And, Mr. Jankovic, it's the next page on your right-hand side. At the top, it says: "After the take-over, all personnel of Croatian and Muslim ethnicity were summoned to interviews by the chief," that would have been Drljaca then, I guess, "... and the option of signing declarations of allegiance to the Republika Srpska was explained to them. They were ... given a reasonable time-limit ... which was extended twice." And then it says: "Additionally, interviews were also conducted with a number of Serbian members of the staff who had not been explicit enough in defining their future work engagement." Do you know what that refers to? Do you know any Serbian members who were interviewed by the chief about, you know, signing the declaration and continuing to work for the new Serbian SJB in Prijedor? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from that period, I don't know anything. What I know now is as they are pensioners and having arguments about the years of service that each of them have, then I know that they can't come to an agreement about which day which one of them came to work or whatever. So I wasn't there and I don't know anything from that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand. The next I want to ask you about --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We need to go to page 14 in the English in e-court and page 12 in the B/C/S in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for you, Mr. Jankovic, if you could go to the next page where there is a little blue sticky-tab at the top. Keep going it's the last one -- yeah. Uh-huh. Yes. Okay. You see this is a section dealing with communications and coded communication.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think at the bottom of your page it talks about open -- about telegrams received in dispatch, both open and coded. But you'll read part 1, this is from the beginning of the year until April 30th. So this appears to be only the numbers for the first four months of the year, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Give me a moment to have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the specificity of war activities, this report is made up on three parts, namely, the part until the 30th of April; the second in the period thereafter; and the third relates to the participation in war activities. Fine. There's a great deal of it. What is it specifically you are asking me about?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I just want to confirm. It seems to me these numbers are referring only to the first four months, from 1 January to 30 April. So when it says coded telegrams dispatched, it was 36 during the first four months of the year?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm getting confused now. Let me tell you the gist of it. I would have to be analysing this document now. This is the gist: All of the dispatches that were written had to have been entered into that book, and when you're writing reports like these, you are consulting these books only. And nobody dared to lie or misrepresent anything because you would have inspection coming to check. And of course mistakes can happen, like the bit where I wrote 1991 instead of 1992. As for the rest, I would have to look into the maths of it, what was meant by each of the figures presented here, and I'm afraid it would take up too much of your time --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- this must have been taken out of one book or other.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I'm not trying to trick you here, and I don't really want to haul out the log-books again because I don't think any of us do --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no doubt about that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But we looked at the one book of coded telegrams early on when I started cross-examining you. And you remember I think the number was about 100 coded telegrams for the entire year of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in your report, which we just looked at before looking at this document, you had 98 coded telegrams for the entire year. And --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I believe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Take my word for it. And here we see 36 -- we see 36 for the --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But evidently this isn't the period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct. This is for the first four months from 1 January to 30 April --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that's probably how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And if you look at the code book I think you -- if you look at the comms log for coded telegrams, you'll see that that works out, meaning that there were approximately 62 sent from the day of the take-over until the end of the year. But I want to go to the next page if we could, page 13, next page in B/C/S, still the same page in English on the lower half. I want to read from this paragraph, please bear with me while I read a long passage and then I'll have a question. "Although the imminent threat of war was very acutely felt in the previous period, the work still had to be done ..." it was talking about up until -- from the 1st of the year until April 30th, "... but it was adversely affected as illustrated by the following: The then-chief of the Public Security Station, appointed by the SDA, was working full steam to further the interest of his party," and that's Mr. Talundzic; right? He's the SDA-appointed chief?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was the chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: "... requesting photocopies of the Communications duty roster so that the only Muslim still employed in the Communications, Mirsad Sahuric," who you've told us about before, "could keep him informed of anything of interest in Communications." Right so far?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then it says: "During this time, the Serbs on the communications staff were covertly --"

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, is that a question or confirmation of what was said here?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please don't interrupt me when I'm getting to my most important point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Because you didn't pose the question. You just asked him to read, and he said yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I said, "Right so far?" And he said, "Yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't pose the question. You just read him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm asking if he agreed what I just read.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me read the next point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: "During this time the Serbs on the Communications staff were covertly organising themselves, carefully monitoring the flow of information through the Communications Centre and reporting about the execution or non-execution of received instructions either to the Executive Committee or to the Banja Luka Centre of Security Services, depending on their assessment." Mr. Jankovic, did you know about this? Did you personally know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: About the Serbs covertly organising themselves, the Serbs on the communications staff covertly organising themselves and reporting to the Executive Committee or Banja Luka centre about the reporting -- about the execution or non-execution of received instructions? Did you know anything about that? I'm talking about from the beginning of the year until the 30th of April.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, as I'm reading it, I have images of pre-war Partisans films in my mind, where everybody from old women and children were participants in the battle. And even the communications service now seems to be involved in this. I had no connections with Talundzic. I spoke very little. He didn't ask me much. And of course I had my specialist line that led to Banja Luka, but there wasn't much that I had to deal with them. The transmission of dispatches, right. And I could have relied on technical assistance from Banja Luka, but their level of equipment was so poor by that time that I couldn't even depend on them for that. So when we're talking about this sort of underground work or covert work, it's like we're talking Partisans all over again, covering and reporting. Come on. Who would I have been doing that with? I didn't know anybody there. I told you that I saw him for the first time during the take-over.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That last sentence you were referring to Simo Drljaca; right? When you said you saw him for the first time during the take-over?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. No but --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And there was nobody else who came from the SDS. Perhaps there was someone whom I didn't know and at any rate since I didn't know the person I wasn't able to be in touch with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
