utterances.text: The next sentence, the last on the English page and going on to the next page in English: "All this was done clandestinely and for obvious reasons there are no records." Mr. Jankovic, I accept that you may have not known anything about this and may not have participated in it, but do you disagree that other Serbs working in the communications centre may have been doing this without you knowing about it, some of your co-workers?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm convinced they have not. This is why: Those who type in the dispatches, none of them, as I said, including Sarac who was too lazy to send the dispatch in question in three different ways, they simply didn't get involved. Their only job was to type things in. There was this Mladen Raus who was a technician. Before him was the Ukrainian guy and later it was Sasa Djukic, I mentioned him here, he was a young guy. This Raus could fix a device or two, but to issue one without me knowing, it was impossible. I knew every device by heart. If there were three radio stations missing, I would notice, let alone a thousand-plus stations. Raus could not have issued anything of that sort. I would have known. As for someone else doing things on the side without telling me, well, they weren't expert enough to fix devices. As for the signalsmen, I didn't even think they'd be able to do something to someone. They simply forwarded their dispatches. I also didn't know that the Sahuric person worked against the Serbs and later on he joined them after the take-over. I think it was his job to do that without any opportunity being given to him to -- whatever he did had to have been noted down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me stop you there. You're saying you didn't know anything about this and you didn't do anything like that. And you're also saying as far as you're concerned you don't believe any of your fellow Serb communication workers at that time could have or would have done something like that. Is that a fair summary?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know positively for myself. I'm convinced for the others, although there is a possibility. My belief is that they didn't do anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. Reading on: "Furthermore, during this time Serbian reserve police stations were being covertly formed and preparations made for the take-over and the Communications personnel took upon themselves to establish communications for this operation. This entailed a lot of work, from attending meetings and assessing requirements, through the drafting of directories of names and code-books to ensuring the necessary equipment ..." So again, if that happened, you're telling us that you didn't know anything about it; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let me say this: These spare or reserve illegal stations he mentioned, was anything done with them? Is there any proof that any of that was included in any particular operation? They may have figured in plans of organisation, but nothing was done with them for me to be able to notice that they were in existence. I wasn't asked to provide any pieces of equipment. Now, whether after the take-over some things were done, well probably. On that day a number of radio stations were used as part of regular police work and used for that purpose. But during the take-over operation, I don't seem to remember any dense radio communication traffic that could not be covered by the pieces we had in regular work. I have always said this. Only in larger-scale operations where additional communication means are required, that was something I must have known. As for anything else, things could have done -- people could have done things that I would not have been aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You remember --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise there is another correction to the transcript. I turn in Serbian. [Interpretation] Page 48, when the witness discussed of the larger-scale operations and then he reverted to smaller-scale or less-important operations. We don't find that in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you hear that, Mr. Jankovic? Is that correct? Did you intend to include smaller-scale operation as well in that part of your answer?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me be clear. I'm saying this: There could have been smaller-scale operations which did not require any auxiliary communication means, and in that case no one would ask anything of me. Under such circumstances, I would have been ignorant of it. However, in this specific case I have never heard of any illegal radio station being used in any operation. I'm positive I have never heard of that. No one ever asked any communication equipment piece of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Just a couple more questions and I'll be done, Mr. Jankovic. You remember telling us about -- after the meeting with Mr. Zupljanin on the 9th of April when there was a discussion about the new insignia, at page 24767 on Monday you told us that Chief Zupljanin told you that you guys, meaning you people in the Prijedor police station, must agree among yourselves about how to resolve this. You can't wait for someone from the outside doing that for you. And you said then Fikret Kadiric, the commander, said, "Sir we cannot do that because some people are spying upon other people. That's the word he used and he pointed the finger at me." Do you remember telling us about that, that Mr. Kadiric accused you of spying?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He used a grammatically incorrect term, but that's the meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is it possible that he suspected you because of some things he'd seen happening in the communications department, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you another thing and then you can compare --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you can tell me in a minute, but can you answer my question first?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said things that had nothing to do with the truth, that were groundless. Only a couple of days later I was summoned by Chief Hasan Talundzic to his office, so I did. Next to him was Fikret Kadiric and a female employee Fikreta Asusic [phoen]. Hasan told me this: "Sefita [phoen] complained that you passed by her on the staircase and that you hit her with your hand." I was completely shocked. I knew it had nothing to do with anything. When I came to after the shock I asked her: "When did that happen?" She said: "The day before yesterday, Monday." And then I recalled. Without a word I went to my office and brought my travel order. On that day I was in Sarajevo and returned late in the evening. I showed it to him and they fell silent. No one ever raised the issue again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was completely untrue. Such things occurred on numerous occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Let me stop you there. But you've seen what Mr. Drljaca put in his report in some detail about the actions taken, he says, by people in the communications department, about the setting up of the reserve police stations. His reports earlier in the year about 300 policemen guarding in Keraterm, Omarska, and Trnopolje. I suggest to you that what happened was you weren't trusted by Mr. Drljaca and the SDS because you were not a political guy, and you've told us how you tried to help your Muslim coworker Mr. Sahuric. So you were out of the loop. You weren't told about these things because the radical Serbs, the extremist Serbs, didn't trust you. Isn't that the logical explanation for why you don't know about any of this, and why you didn't know about the combat activity that the Prijedor SJB police were involved in? That makes sense, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say this first. We were a small operative unit. In a cocoon so to speak. We didn't have much contact with others. Our office was locked and no one could enter except for us and the chief, who came rarely, once or twice a year. We were a closed unit. No one ever inquired about work. Fikret could not have known anything because he didn't use to come in. As for one of the signalsmen telling him something, I don't think it was very likely, and this includes Sahuric. As for the politicians, we were so remote to them that I wonder whether they knew we existed. They must have known that there were communications departments in the MUP, but it ended with that. If you want to know anything more, you should ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jankovic. I don't have any more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a few questions for you. They had to do with the questions put to you by the Prosecutor. I'll start with the document in front of you, which is P00689.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have page 13 in the Serbian version. The ERN number is 00633760. It's the next page. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drljaca in the second paragraph reads --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could we please wait for the English translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: He says that Mr. Fakovic used his independent channels to inform Chief Talundzic or to report to him. Just one moment, please. We don't have the English translation. I think it is page 14 in the English. Mr. Drljaca asserts that Mr. Mirsad Sahuric independently report to Chief Talundzic. The Prosecutor read out this part to you and you provided an answer about the document. Is this part about Sahuric correct and what was your knowledge of his activities at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sahuric, everything in this document is incomprehensible to me, including the mention of Sahuric. I am convinced that Sahuric was a good worker and that he wasn't prone to do such things. Even if I had known that, how could I have -- well, I went to his house once or twice and I even sent Raus and there was Sarac. I told them to go and visit the family. We couldn't have been extremists, the both of us, to be on such good terms. I even sent Mladen Raus and Dusko Sarac also went to his house. I visited him twice before he left with the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't accept that he didn't do his job properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, is what Mr. Drljaca mentions correct, in your view?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I said, this only reminds me of the old Partisans movies and heros of Mirko and Slavko. They all joined hands in order to fight the villain, including the children, and this document reminds me of that. The entire communications department was so small and there was so little leeway that things simply had to go through the books. I couldn't issue a piece of equipment without people knowing. We were always in a small enclosed space like this, and we knew nothing of the outside world.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We don't have much time, could you please try and answer my questions briefly.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm afraid it's impossible to answer this kind of question briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, you were asked by the Prosecutor a moment ago about the participation of the police in combat. When it comes to more important operations involving the police, were there any changes made to the communications network? Was the communication department obliged to do something?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. In the period before the take-over there were no such operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about combat, if the police are engaged in combat, is there anything for the communications department to do anything? Do you need to issue additional equipment, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. With greater numbers of people, you need more devices, and the person in charge of organising should plan for such a contingency and then they would always ask for more equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And if there were smaller things going on not requiring many policemen, in other words, to carry out regular routine activities, did they require any additional effort?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because only the equipment that was in standard use was then relied on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor cited some figures from Mr. Drljaca's reports. What is your knowledge concerning the document and the figures put forth by Mr. Drljaca and what is your impression? Did he inflate the numbers or are the numbers too small, too low?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the figures that we saw in the two documents, they're not rounded off, but I don't think he changed anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I was discussing the other figures, the number of policemen, radio stations.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't resemble anything. It's unrealistic. As for the dispatches, I think it tallies with my figures more or less, according to the books. But as for his numbers of policemen, et cetera, no way. Thirteen hundred policemen? Where did he come up with that? It's an exaggeration. Before the war the entire station had 230 employees, including the crime department, communications department. The crime department had up to 30, the police over a hundred. So the maximum could have been 250. From that you need to take off the number of Muslims who left and some Serbs. So how did he come up with the figure of 180 active-duty policemen? It's ridiculously unreal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor showed you another document before the one we just discussed. P2394, tab 138. The last page, please. At the bottom you say that the overall telegram traffic was by 62 per cent lower than the previous year?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Is -- does this relate to the whole year because this was your report for 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Does this also include what you said before, which is that there was only one-third of the overall traffic compared to the previous years?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one-third would be 33 per cent. When I mentioned it to you, I wasn't familiar with these numbers. Now when I look at them, that -- if we deduct 62 it would leave us with 38 per cent and one-third would be 33. So it was my assessment, and I wasn't off much it seems. As for what period, I don't know. As far as I'm familiar with it, you compare a quarter to a quarter or half a year to half a year. So it has to be an equivalent. That's the principal used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But report of yours covers a full year, if you look at the cover page?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the report about the coding, yes. Those were annual reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, in the first three months or let's say until the 30th of April, 1992, were there any reductions? What were the figures before the 30th April compared to the previous year? Was the network down at any point in time before the take-over?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was. Before the political problems occurred, everything went down. We no longer purchased new equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I meant to ask you about the period when it was quiet before the take-over, when you compare that period, the quiet period, with the period in 1992, were there any discrepancies?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any significant differences? I'm asking you about the quiet period.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were changes in 1992 as well. I'm not trying to avoid answering, but let's take 1985 or 1986, five years before this date, we always had about 100.000 dispatches a year. In other words, 1991 was also a significant change and here we have another reduction by 62 per cent compared to 1991, even though Prijedor was one of the smaller centres. So it was a period of stagnation, although it's difficult to say anything more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, the Prosecutor asked -- showed you some documents which did not originate from your -- in your communications centre and we saw some entries. Can you tell us what would be a relevant piece of information about the number of sent and received dispatches and the rate of success in terms of successful transmission. Where could one find such figures?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nowhere. We only kept records in normal conditions. If we go back to the dispatch of a moment ago with my ellips is. It went through our regular communications channels but came back my Telefax. We were circumvented, in other words, and such entries were not made. If something didn't go through, it was also noted down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But such an unsuccessful dispatch, would it have been assigned a number?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are the books that I am not familiar with. Mira perhaps kept such records. I suppose she did, but I didn't worry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: From the figures shown to you by the Prosecutor, can you conclude whether there was a successful attempt to send a dispatch or not?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. What I could see in the books I was shown includes not only dispatches but documents of all sorts sent through different channels.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the speakers not overlap and pause. Interpreter's note that a couple of questions and answers weren't interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We do speak the same language so there was an overlap. I asked you if the books that the Prosecutor showed you made a clear indication of whether a dispatch had been transmitted or not.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat what I said. Normally something like that would not have been an issue so that there wasn't a box made appositely for that. There was a column which stated remarks or notes, but there wasn't anything entered there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, the Prosecutor further showed you a number of documents which indicated an exchange between Mr. Zupljanin, that's to say the CSB of Banja Luka, and the SJB of Prijedor. I'll show you P00682 now. It will appear on your screen shortly. If I remember correctly we don't have the right -- I don't have the right page of transcript. You, it seems to me, commented on this dispatch of Simo Drljaca's as being an impertinent one or brazen. So would you say that this dispatch reflects the sort of conduct or demeanour that a chief should assume when addressing someone?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look at this. It says we are unable to conduct an inquiry into the stated death of a number of Muslim individuals in Koricanske Stijene because all the policemen who escorted the convoy for Travnik on that date were at the battle-field in Han Pijesak. Well, this wasn't in Mars if it was in Han Pijesak. I'm sure that this could have been dealt with, and it is really inappropriate of him to state such reasons to his immediate superior. To me it is cheeky, it is brazen, and inappropriate. And I can tell you that I saw similar writings of his before. It is really irresponsible to say that you are unable to deal with a matter that is as serious as this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So quite apart from the fact that these policemen, as it says here, were deployed on a mission, is -- or was there a record kept of policemen in the Prijedor public security station and their data?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that and I don't know who was deployed to Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You misunderstand me. My question was: Were the particulars of individual policemen kept on the record in Prijedor and should a superior inquire of them?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I think that the commander would have a record or perhaps the personnel service. Somebody would at any rate. Well, you see, I had appropriate records for my communications officers that I used when I was drawing up reports, and I'm sure they had for theirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor went on to ask you about the relationship between Zupljanin and Simo Drljaca. He asked you if you had an example to give where Chief Zupljanin's instructions or orders were not complied with. Do you know of any fuel tanker trucks from or to Banja Luka passing through Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do think that I spoke about this, either to the Defence or the Prosecution. I do recall this once when there was a shortage of fuel, which was a general occurrence at the time, and they got hold of a fuel tanker. I think it was diesel fuel. And Simo was told that this was intended for those in Banja Luka, but he said, "Oh, they'll get by. We'll keep this for our own purposes," although it was not initially intended for us, and I did find it inconceivable at the time. I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry I didn't quite understand you now. Can you explain this to us. Who took the fuel tanker and it belonged to whom?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said we took it from the Banja Luka people -- well, I can't speak of any persons because I don't know who it was. I only know that we had a shortage of fuel and all of a sudden we had a supply of fuel. And then when I asked about it, we -- it was said that we had taken it over from the Banja Luka people. Apparently my idea of it was that this tanker was intended for the Banja Luka fellow policemen. I suppose it had to do with the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And who was it who misappropriated it? I don't mean physically, but who ordered that this be taken?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again I repeat, I heard about it. I didn't see it, but I would say that nobody would dare do such a thing without the approval of one's superior, and the superior must have been Simo. I don't think any of the commanders would have ordered it. Perhaps I should be considering that possibility rather than blame it all on the late Simo. But my idea would be that it was Simo who was behind it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have some 20 minutes left, but I do believe it's time for our break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, so we would return for you to wrap up and then we have some housekeeping matters with which to deal before we adjourn for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, I have several short questions left for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown P00377, which is behind tab 52 of the Prosecution binder. Please enlarge it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor read a portion of the document for you. I will read the part I'm interested in: "This is to inform you that all the workers who have not signed the solemn oath, or rather, who have not declared their intention to continue working in public security stations as units of organisation, the Banja Luka CSB of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina MUP have -- are to have that employment terminated as at 15 April 1992." And then you did say it, but could you remind me whose signature this was?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said and I'm convinced that it's Milutin Cadjo, the then commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It goes on to read. The chief has decided --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: Has expressed his agreement with and then employment or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the interpretation says "emphasized."

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I can read there he came to an agreement or agreed to something with someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was Cadjo's immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cadjo's?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the Prijedor public security station.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure. There was jostling for position there. There was Dujo Jankovic who was a commander and then -- well, I believe that Jankovic was his senior, though I know that Cadjo was a commander for a period as well in our building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And who was their superior?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Simo, Simo was. There was nobody in between them. There was them and then Simo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Answering to the questions put by the Prosecutor in page 21 you spoke of Simo Drljaca. You described him. You gave us an illustration, and there's a part of what you said missing, so would you please now in answering my question answer fully. Whenever Simo wanted to shift responsibility onto someone he would consult people, ask them, but whenever he needed to have something done, that's where your sentence doesn't end. Whenever he was to gain or get something for himself, what did you say then?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I remember I was saying that. Yes, I knew what I meant. I just have to put it in words. I did take the example of, I believe, parents and children. Whenever he wanted the responsibility to lie with somebody else, he would be inquiring and in consulting people. But when he wanted something to be done and he didn't want many people to know about it, then he would set about it on his own. You did mention fuel, that quantity of fuel, if what I heard was true. Well, he didn't call the chief of the centre to ask him: Chief, can we please steal your supply of fuel -- or whoever it was who did that. I mean, I don't know if it was him. That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, in respect of the regular period before these events, whenever the chief of the station had to make important decisions or have important decisions implemented, would he be briefing the collegium about all this? And I'm asking about the pre-Simo Drljaca period. Was this standard practice?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Whatever was of some significance was discussed and agreed at the collegium meeting. Only if it had to do with strictly police business, then it would be the commanders and chiefs talking and I wouldn't be joining their discussion because it wasn't my lot, but I would be there. Of course there were moments when I wasn't present at these meetings, and then I wouldn't know anything. So I wasn't a participant, but I was present at the collegium meeting and would hear. As for the latter period, that wasn't the case, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Drljaca say that you should adhere to the decisions taken by Chief Zupljanin, and did he give you any sort of instruction on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Far from it. Not at all. Let me be more specific. He didn't say either that we shouldn't be complying with what he said. He just gave us our tasks and told us what we were to do. And as for him addressing us on any issue, well, that individual didn't figure in that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Jankovic, when it came to the workings of the public security station during Mr. Drljaca's time there, did they depart from standard practice? You said at one point that there was this departure from standard procedure by 95 per cent you said in some context. So would you say that this was true also for the running of the public security station while Mr. Drljaca was there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't just him. There were other policemen who were police illiterates, the way I called them. It wasn't just him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. Mr. Jankovic, your answer wasn't recorded properly. I asked you what the difference was between the period before Mr. Drljaca and after Mr. Drljaca took up his position in the station. You said what you had to say but it wasn't interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me just say briefly that in the normal period there were meetings, including the collegium, and the superior officer was complied with. Whatever they were doing they had to comply with what he said. And every policeman or member of the station would be doing their proper job and report back to the superior. None of that existed when he took up his position. I don't know if he had any consultations with some of his associates. What I can tell you is that I and some other people were not part of his consultations, plans, and such-like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor also asked you if you knew when it was that Mr. Simo Drljaca was replaced. I think you did say that you wouldn't be able to pin-point the date, and do you know who it was who removed Simo Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I only know that he went to Bijeljina, returned, and then left for good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When discussing the Omarska and Keraterm centres, the Prosecutor asked you about the growing numbers of these people. You were talking about the fact that both sides were preparing for clashes. In that period of time, early April [as interpreted], was it known the number of Croats and Muslims who had taken part in these activities, i.e., attacks on Prijedor? And was there available information about how many of such organised units there were?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the number --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the question needs some clarification. It says: "In that period of time, early April, was it known the number of Croats and Muslims who had taken part in these activities, i.e., attacks on Prijedor?" Now, I understand the attack on Prijedor was May the 30th, so nobody could have known in April 1992 who was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think I mentioned April, but let me be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, at that point in time in Prijedor when the hostilities broke out and when these centres of Keraterm and Omarska were set up, what were the assessments of the numbers of Muslims and Croats who had been organised in these units?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How many individuals took part in the attack?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No. How many people were organised into formations as a result of responding to mobilisation call-ups.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Prijedor, well I don't know the number. I can give you some guesses. I do know that the lesser part of them did not participate. I know that there were 49.000 Muslims in the municipality. There were fewer Croats. So let's say that there were 50.000 of them. Let's say that half of them were women, then you're left with 25.000. And let's say that 40 per cent of them would be able-bodied because you would have the elderly and children. And then if you take into account those who deserted as well, there might have been those, you would end up with a figure of 10.000. Or let me give you this other view of mine. The Kozarac police substation which belonged to the Prijedor station covered 22.000 inhabitants before the war. Of these 22.000, there were very few who weren't Muslims. There were Serbs, Ukrainians, Croats, but a handful in all. I don't think there were more than 2.000 of them. So if we take Kozarac alone to have had 20.000 Muslims and then half of them men and a third of those were participants because of the rest being children and elderly, again you would end up with some 3- to 4.000 persons as active-duty people. But that would merely be my maths. I didn't see any lists anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you said there was a small number of them who did not respond to the mobilisation, small number of Muslims. What did you have in mind? Did you have the JNA mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. For example, I and my friend Djeric, who was an electrical engineer working in the mine, when the unrest period occurred before the take-over he took his wife and went to Germany. He found work there. Not everyone was able to do that, but he avoided being drafted. So he was an able-bodied man who left and lived a good life elsewhere. There were many such people but not everyone could do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you discussed mobilisation, did you have in mind the Muslim TO mobilisation or some other?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I even saw on tape that everyone had their own mobilisation. All I could see on that tape was that there was a mobilisation. Whose it was and how many people there were I don't know. I could see people there, but how many people they called, how many people they gathered, that's something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor showed you a number of documents discussing Serb preparations for the beginning of activities. I'll show you 2D00108. You compared those preparations to the race to the moon between the US and the USSR?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just as an illustration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We have a criminal report submitted by the Ministry of the Interior. Could we please go to page 3 in the Serbian version. In the explanation of reasons it says that in late 1991 and early 1992 organised by the -- the organisation of Prijedor SDA is being approached by a number of people who wanted to have arms. For that purpose they began collecting financial means to purchase weapons with the help of, among others, the so-called Prijedor Crisis Staff comprised exclusively of citizens of Muslim nationality. Certain people left for Germany. My question is this: Did you have any knowledge or information that at the same time the Serbs were forming their Crisis Staff, the Muslims had their own parallel organisation preparing for a take-over?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't familiar with the whole situation. I could just see details here and there. Suljo the colleague of mine, and who was a neighbour, too, complained to me, and he was relatively wealthy just before the war because he had poker machines in police facilities. It was -- he was -- he never wanted to give away much money and me complained to me that they asked for a lot. He basically told me that he had to provide money, and he wasn't the only one that must have been asked. The -- when the shooting occurred during the attack on Prijedor, for example, I could hear the fighting. When you hear gun-shots you could tell when a particular rifle was used called a Singapore rifle which had a higher-frequency bullet sound like a wasp. Our military and the police did not have any other rifles save for the semi-automatic produced by the Zastava factory and the so-called Kalashnikov, the automatic rifle. They sound the same. When I heard what I did during the first few days, I heard such sounds. It must mean that those rifles were purchased from somewhere. So there were weapons around. It's not like they were without any weapons all of a sudden. As far as I know, there were up to three companies involved, one across the bridge, one next to the Sedelos [phoen] facility, and another one. And if a company has about a hundred people, I suppose they didn't send people into combat unarmed and it takes preparation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, please focus on my questions. I have very few left. You have already provided me with an answer. The Prosecutor showed you P2394 a moment ago and I want you to see it again. It's tab 137. Apologies. It's P689 actually. Next page, please. This is Mr. Drljaca's document. He mentioned 400 police members. You've already told us what you think of his figures. And that -- those 400 were supposed to be in Cirkin Polje. You told us what your assessment was of the number of people. When you issued the IDs, were you given 400 or 500 such forms approximately?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the cards were packed in small boxes resembling a cigarette box. It was about this size and when I finished it went down to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could that have included 400 IDs?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Impossible. They didn't only ask for those on the first day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Krgovic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you already said that it was impossible that there were that many?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Not everyone got it the first evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this and please let me finish before answering. You described the people you saw in different uniforms and you said there were all kinds. You said that some had police uniforms and then there were others. In your assessment which group was bigger?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there were all sorts of colours. There were three or four different military uniforms, types of uniforms, the camouflage, the regular ones, the old for the reserve force, the olive-drab. There were many without any uniform or in just a shirt. Some were in jute clothes resembling those that were issued to the reserve police force a while ago, and I didn't see any of my colleagues there, people who worked with me. I knew all of them because I was there every day with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Compared to the overall number or -- what would be the percentage, 15, 20 per cent of those you saw?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to say. It's half dark and I'm writing out forms. I told you there was a short meeting and then Simo gave me the forms. I didn't go out. It was getting dark. I would have to guess whatever I said. There may have been 20 per cent of our active personnel, but it's best not to say anything because there could have been two times as many or as few.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That's all right if you can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, I have just one small question for you. You told us I think a couple of days back during your testimony here that at the meeting that was held on the evening of the 29th of April before the take-over of Prijedor, a great number of people were present that night. You mentioned that a number of police officers were there. I think you also mentioned that some paramilitary forces were there, and you also mentioned that there were two army officers. Do you recall what you told us?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, you said a meeting and then I thought you were thinking of the 29th concerning the take-over. And then from the latter part of your question, I realised that you had a different thing in mind. I thought you meant the meeting concerning the dispatch at 2.00 p.m., and the other thing in the evening -- well, do you have in mind the other part in Cirkin Polje and that you refer to it as a meeting? In Cirkin Polje?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I do indeed, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I'm not discussing the part at 2.00 p.m., but the one following 8.00 p.m. I did use the term "a small meeting," but it wasn't an official meeting. I'll try to illustrate. I got there, it was a pre-fab building the size of this room surrounded by a courtyard three times as big. And there were many people there, maybe a hundred, 120 in different groups discussing. I got in as a junior manager. I went in to see where the others were and I found the commander there, the chief of the crime service, and Hasan Talundzic, and Fikret. Then Simo appeared, I could see him. I didn't talk to him because I didn't know him, but others did. And since -- it became an office as a matter of fact -- I'll try to slow down. It was the office of the local commune secretary who was in charge of issuing birth certificates, et cetera, there was a table there. And people in charge sat down. Simo said, "My name is Simo Drljaca. I was sent by the SDS." We introduced ourselves to them, and he seemed to know the people from the police, and I was always sort of on the side. I was present but I didn't participate in the conversation because it came upon me all of a sudden. I could observe what was going on there, and I can't tell you word for word what they said. But those four or five of them agreed that it should be sent to town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. You see, my question goes to the following aspects of those events; namely, who had organised all of this? It must have taken some co-ordinated efforts to gather all these people together with the purpose of taking over Prijedor during that night and in the early morning hours of the following day. Who in your understanding was behind this?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, when you say that it was co-ordinated, it is my opinion too. It is impossible it was a mere coincidence. That's the first conclusion. The second, if Simo arrived, some, including myself, didn't know him because he was not a familiar person around town. Maybe half of the policemen did know him, the other half did not. If he arrived saying he was sent by the SDS, their involvement is obvious. If there was this major there whom I mentioned who asked for hand-held devices, and there was another military person whose rank I no longer recall, and I could see them even though it was getting dark, there may have been more, it must mean that the army was involved too. If someone called me through the communications centre, because we always had such situations in which we would be called to do something without any previous planning; for example, the chief can say, "Bring together the whole station." And then the secretary does that. They would do that through the communications centre to get to me. Perhaps they would call ten people and those ten would call those under them. It didn't strike me as unusual the way we were summoned, but I don't know who took part in all that. I never bothered to find out. I did see all of those people there and it seemed to me they were acting in concert. No one seemed surprised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. So your answer is that you are not able to form an opinion about who had organised all of this. You mentioned that the army was there, that the SDS obviously played a role, the police was involved as well, and possibly a number of others. But you do not have any opinion about who had organised the meeting in the following events; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that there were people from different organisational parts. I learned in the course of my work not to think about things I shouldn't be. It's not up to me to think about what the Prosecutor is trying to do. I know that if I'm summoned somewhere, I'm to sit there and await for my tasks to be given to me. I'm not the man in charge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry to intervene, and I do it with great trepidation, but there was something in an earlier part of the answer that's extremely unclear to me and seems inconsistent and I would like to ask about. It's at page 71 -- page 70, line 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, Judge Harhoff asked you a question, and in your answer you said: "I got there, it was a pre-fab building the size of this room surrounded by a courtyard three times as big. There were people there, maybe a hundred, 120 in different groups discussing. I got in as a junior manager. I went in to see where the others were and I found the commander there, the chief of the service, Hasan Talundzic, and Fikret." Now, are you talking -- you're not talking about Cirkin Polje, are you? Because I had the understanding that there weren't any Muslims at Cirkin Polje on the night of the 29th of April.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either you did not understand me or maybe I spoke too fast. I did say what you said, but what I meant to say that it was Fikret and Hasan of course were not there. That is probably what was missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. That's what I thought was the case. I just wanted to be sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, I too actually wondered about it, and it makes a huge difference of course. So you confirm that there were no Muslims present at the meeting that night or at the gathering?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's good that we cleared it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks a lot. Thanks, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: There was something arising, Mr. Krgovic? You seemed to be about to rise?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There was one thing I had requested, Your Honour, when the witness went home if he could look for his ID card that he had prepared that night. He thought he might still have it, and I'd requested that the Trial Chamber direct Victim Witness to co-ordinate with him on that in the event that he might be able to find it and loan it to us to make a copy and enter it into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jankovic, Mr. Hannis has just reminded you of something that he requested yesterday. So the -- such directions as are necessary for the -- to facilitate the Chamber now makes. So you can expect to be contacted by, I suppose by VWS in terms of facilitating this. And your testimony is now at an end and you are released. We thank you for coming to assist the Tribunal and we wish you a safe journey back home. The Chamber has certain procedural matters with which to deal so it isn't rising at the moment, and I would ask the usher to please escort you from the courtroom. Thank you, sir. Did you wish to say something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I just wanted to ask you something. I already said that it's not a problem for me to provide a copy. There could be a technical matter, though, because I need to copy it first. In any case, if there is someone who could call me, you know my phone number, and then we could meet and hand-over the copy. There was another thing. I was trying to remember things and the ID is like a booklet, you can open it. On the right-hand side is the same text that used to be on the Yugoslav IDs, which is that the authorised official is entitled to verify one's identity, bring in persons, seize weapons, et cetera, in accordance with the law. This is quite standard for any police force in the world. It was on the right-hand side once you open the booklet. It read: Official ID. And on the left-hand side there was first and last name and a few other details. That was it. On the right-hand side was the text. On the back side there was nothing. Perhaps someone should get in touch with me and then we'll make a copy. There's no reason for me not to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before we rise for the day, the Chamber wishes to note that next week's schedule will be subject to some changes in order to accommodate two Plenary sessions which have been -- Plenary session of Judges which have been scheduled for Wednesday and Thursday. So in order to ensure that the witness next week completes his testimony before we adjourn for two weeks, according to the last published schedule in alternating trials, the Trial Chamber is making arrangements to sit an extra session on the afternoon of both Monday and Tuesday. Now, on Wednesday we are scheduled to sit in the afternoon and we need to commence the hearing in the morning and then rise in the middle of the day to reconvene in the afternoon after a break of approximately two and a half hours. The details of this are still being worked out. And on Thursday, when we are also scheduled to sit in the afternoon, we will sit as normal, and we expect to sit regular hours on Friday morning. Parties should note that the precise details of this would be communicated the -- by the Legal Officers by way of e-mail. And if I may a moment, there's a note that I'm just seeing. The only thing I would add is that the concern of the Chamber remains that no court time is lost so that wherever gaps or otherwise occurs, the Chamber fully expects that the counsel would make every effort to ensure that the time is fully spent. Did counsel -- I understand that the OTP has certain scheduling matters themselves to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Your last comment sort of addressed what I wanted to raise, Your Honour. Given what had happened during the last alternation between this trial and the Haradinaj trial, where there was a gap, we did manage to get one witness in for one day. But I guess just in anticipating the possibility that something might happen again the next time, we just wanted to alert everybody that if that happens, we would ask the Defence to let us know if they will be able to bring in somebody on short notice and who that might be so we can deal with that in the event that we might be sitting sometime between the 24th of October and the 4th of November in case Haradinaj is not sitting for any reason whatever. That was the first point. And the second was, Your Honour, regarding the next witness from the Defence, SZ-009. I understand he's here already and has been here for a little while. We would request if there's any proofing note we have it as soon as possible because his 65 ter is four brief paragraphs and rather vague. One says: "The witness will speak about his visit to Prijedor during the summer of 1992. Furthermore, he'll testify about his stay in Doboj in May 1992." That's not very informative and given that we don't have a statement from him and haven't had an interview with him, it would assist if we can have -- and he's not willing to speak to us, it would assist if we could have some further details in our preparations for his cross-examine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as for the proofing note, my colleague Mr. Aleksic is dealing with that and he will send it in the course of the day. What the Prosecutor said latterly is partly untrue. The witness [as interpreted] did speak to the witness back in 2004, and they do have a pretty detailed outline of his future testimony. This would be the second time that they are seeing the witness and there should be no doubt as to what this witness will speak to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So with that we take the adjournment to reconvene -- I think we sit in this courtroom next week at 9.00 Monday morning, and I trust everyone has a safe weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 17th day of October, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.
